patterns.name: The 'Delve' family (Kobak excess words)
patterns.definition: Stylistic verbs and adjectives whose corpus frequency spiked abruptly after November 2022; almost entirely stylistic rather than content-bearing. Flag on density, not on a single occurrence.

examples.before: By meticulously delving into the intricate web connecting [...] and [...], this comprehensive chapter takes a deep dive into their involvement as significant risk factors for [...]

patterns.notes: Source's frequency ratios vs pre-LLM baseline: delves r = 28.0, underscores r = 13.8, showcasing r = 10.7 (Kobak et al., Science Advances 2025; 15M+ PubMed abstracts; >= 13.5% of 2024 abstracts LLM-processed, up to 40% in MDPI/Frontiers). Full list of 900 excess words: berenslab/llm-excess-vocab on GitHub. Called 'delve-speak'. 'Human writers say delve' — a single hit is not proof.

patterns.name: Focal words (ChatGPT-3.5, 'Why does ChatGPT delve so much?')
patterns.definition: Twenty-one lexical items that spiked in Scientific English and are overused by ChatGPT-3.5; a second, partly overlapping list from the Kobak excess words. Count occurrences per 500 words and compare against the 'excess band'.
patterns.notes: arxiv 2412.11385. The Delve Audit exercise uses an 18-word subset: delve, intricate, meticulously, realm, pivotal, navigate, landscape, tapestry, resonate, testament, underscore, showcasing, compelling, paramount, crucial, foster, elevate, surpass. The 30-second field check uses the tightest subset (delve, intricate, pivotal, realm, meticulously, navigate, tapestry) and only counts it 'in a non-academic context'.

patterns.name: The 'Tapestry' nouns (metaphors for abstract prestige)
patterns.definition: Grand abstract nouns used metaphorically to lend borrowed grandeur to flat subjects.
patterns.notes: Quoted editor stance (The Conversation, 2024): 'I no longer believe there's a way to innocently use the word tapestry in an essay; if the word tapestry appears, it was generated by ChatGPT' — i.e. 'tapestry' alone is treated as near-decisive by some editors; the rest of the list is a density signal. 'Rich tapestry' also appears in the 30-second check as a promotional-adjective example.

patterns.name: Corporate-inflation adjectives
patterns.definition: Adjectives that were once working members of the language and are now 'radioactive' — buzzword intensifiers applied indiscriminately.
patterns.notes: Sources cited: Walter Writes AI; Yours AI Slop.

patterns.name: Inflated verbs
patterns.definition: Verbs of corporate uplift chosen over the plain verb (use, help, make, look at).

patterns.name: Signposting filler phrases
patterns.definition: Stock transition and emphasis phrases that announce a point instead of making it; the LLM's verbal tics of transition.
cues: Play a (vital / pivotal / crucial / significant) role in…
A nuanced take / a nuanced understanding of…
Sit with that for a moment

examples.before: By meticulously delving into the intricate web connecting [...] and [...], this comprehensive chapter takes a deep dive into their involvement as significant risk factors for [...]

patterns.notes: 'The more of these you count per 500 words, the darker the probability.' Running catalogs: DeGPT tells; a fourteen-phrase editor's quick-flag list (YourTango).

patterns.name: Closing ritual phrases ('preachy conclusions')
patterns.definition: A formulaic wrap-up phrase that opens a final paragraph or sentence, tying the piece in a bow; often followed by advice or exhortation.
cues: Remember, when doing X it's important to consider…
As we navigate [X], it's essential that we…
patterns.notes: OpenAI developers complained publicly of inability to suppress these 'preachy conclusions' (OpenAI Community Forum). Also one of the 12 items in the 30-second check: 'A closing In summary / In conclusion / Ultimately… wrap'.

patterns.name: The Negated Contrast ('It's not X, it's Y')
patterns.definition: A contrastive reframe (negative parallelism): deny a lesser framing and then assert the grander one — 'not (just/merely) X, (but/—/it's) Y'. Detect the negation + contrast pair across a dash, semicolon, period or 'but'.
cues: not A — not B — not C; but X, Y, and Z

examples.before: It's not just about efficiency — it's about transformation.
This isn't just a product. It's a revolution.
We're not merely building software; we're rewriting the rules.
Credit card fraud isn't just evolving — it's accelerating.

patterns.notes: Source: 'Perhaps the single most diagnostic rhetorical move'; Blake Stockton calls it the 'most prominent AI writing tell' (blakestockton.com/dont-write-like-ai-1-101-negation); Wikipedia gives 'negative parallelisms' its own section. 'The move scales fractally: whole posts are built out of it, stacked in series of three.' Especially GPT-characteristic. Rewrite rule (Negation Hunt): restate as a direct affirmative. The article's own subtitle is 'It's not X. It's Y.'

patterns.name: Negation-tricolon armature
patterns.definition: Three negated items in parallel followed by the affirmed triple: 'not A — not B — not C; but X, Y, and Z'. The negated contrast fused with the rule of three; typical of AI-assisted LinkedIn writing.
cues: not A — not B — not C; but X, Y, and Z

examples.before: not A — not B — not C; but X, Y, and Z

patterns.notes: Source attributes the observation to Copy Posse. Distinct from the single negated contrast and from the plain tricolon.

patterns.name: The Tricolon / Rule of Three (algorithmic flattening)
patterns.definition: Strings of three parallel phrases, nearly always equal in length and punctuated identically — often three one- or two-word fragments each closed with a period. Not the classical Ciceronian tricolon but its mechanical version.
cues: No fluff. No filler. No stress.
Dream big. Start small. Scale fast.
Learn it. Own it. Live it.

examples.before: Fast. Simple. Effective.
No fluff. No filler. No stress.
Dream big. Start small. Scale fast.
Learn it. Own it. Live it.

patterns.notes: Also appears as 'paragraph tricolons' in email (Gmelius) — a whole paragraph consisting of the triple. Claude is 'less prone to the triplet-closing and tricolon pattern than ChatGPT'. Item in the 30-second check: 'A tricolon of parallel short phrases'. Wikipedia calls the participial-tail construction a 'rule-of-three' variant.

patterns.name: Uniform sentence length (low burstiness)
patterns.definition: Sentence lengths cluster tightly around a metronomic median (14–22 words) with small variance; no short declaratives punctuating long clausal ones.
patterns.notes: GPTZero's original detection signal: 'models formulaically use the same rule to choose the next word in the sentence, leading to low burstiness'. Threshold in the 30-second check: 'Uniform sentence length across a paragraph (burstiness < ~0.5)'. Exercise: chart sentence length sentence-by-sentence against Dillard/Baldwin/Ruefle. Note the ESL false positive: non-native writers naturally produce lower-perplexity text.

patterns.name: Low perplexity (predictable next word)
patterns.definition: Every next word is the one a language model would expect; the text never surprises token-by-token. Manifests as safe, expected collocations and truisms.
patterns.notes: Perplexity 'measures how surprised a language model is by the next word'; LLM text is low and uniform, human text spikes. Backbone of GPTZero, ZeroGPT, Copyleaks, Originality.AI, Writer. Truisms are chosen 'because they have the lowest cross-entropy loss — they are the safest tokens'.

patterns.name: The Bad-Subject Problem
patterns.definition: The grammatical subject of the sentence is not the actual topic of the sentence; the real agent or idea is buried in an object or modifier.

examples.before: Readers are better guided when the subject matches the main idea
examples.after: Choosing the right subject keeps the writing clear and focused

patterns.notes: Shreya Shankar (sh-reya.com/blog/ai-writing). Before = AI-written, after = human-rewritten. Its hallmark is the orphaned demonstrative (listed separately).

patterns.name: Orphaned demonstratives
patterns.definition: 'This', 'that', 'these' used as a sentence subject with no clear referent — typically 'This highlights…' or 'This underscores…' opening a sentence after a paragraph of mixed claims.

examples.before: This highlights… (without a clear antecedent)

patterns.notes: Named as the hallmark of the bad-subject problem and as its own item in the 30-second check: 'Orphaned demonstratives (This highlights… without a clear antecedent)'.

patterns.name: The Participial Tail
patterns.definition: A trailing present-participle phrase (', marking…', ', underscoring…', ', highlighting…') appended to a complete clause that merely restates or inflates the main clause.

examples.before: The initiative represented a significant shift, marking a pivotal moment in the evolution of…
This approach has transformed the field, underscoring its importance for future research.

patterns.notes: Wikipedia's guide treats it as a 'rule-of-three' construction with many variants. Often carries a Kobak word (underscoring, marking, showcasing) and puffed-up significance in the same clause.

patterns.name: Hypotactic smoothness (no fragments, no misbehaviour)
patterns.definition: Every sentence resolves grammatically: no fragments, (mostly) no comma splices, no anacoluthon, no broken-off constructions. The surface is perfect and therefore flat.
patterns.notes: Neil Clarke on Clarkesworld submissions: 'they are boring. They are flat… no subtext or layers'. Pairs with 'Oxford commas, zero contractions, near-perfect grammar'. Do not cure this by injecting deliberate typos (see the paranoia-spiral anti-goal).

patterns.name: Five-paragraph-essay shape at any length
patterns.definition: Intro + three body sections + recap, imposed even on 100-word answers; the ChatGPT default of 'intro + triplet structure + closing recap'.
patterns.notes: AI for Lifelong Learners: 'high school essay vibes'. Listed as a ChatGPT fingerprint ('Default to intro + triplet structure + closing recap'). See also section-level recap and closing ritual phrases.

patterns.name: Section-level recap (summary closes every subsection)
patterns.definition: Each section or subsection ends with a mini-summary that restates what the section just said, often verbatim; in papers the closing paragraph reproduces the paper's own claims.
patterns.notes: Source: 'Section summaries close every subsection (In summary, Overall)' and, in academic writing, 'Section summaries that reproduce the paper's own claims verbatim in closing paragraphs'. Related to the German-medical-essay finding that expert detection was driven by 'redundancy, repetition'.

patterns.name: Excessive signposting (telegraphing every move)
patterns.definition: Meta-announcements of the document's own plan before doing it: 'First, we'll look at… Second, we'll examine… Finally, we'll conclude by…'.

examples.before: First, we'll look at… Second, we'll examine… Finally, we'll conclude by…

patterns.notes: 'The model telegraphs every move. Real essays find their own weather.' Tolerable in long technical documents; a tell in short pieces and essays.

patterns.name: Hedge-and-reassure (stacked hedges)
patterns.definition: A qualifier immediately followed by a reassurance, often three hedges stacked in a single sentence before any claim is made.

examples.before: While this may vary, generally speaking, in most cases, it's worth noting that…

patterns.notes: Identified 'in Claude especially' (Context-link). Claude fingerprint: 'Heavier hedging register: It's worth noting, While this may vary, Generally speaking, In many cases', plus 'more likely to decline or signal uncertainty'.

patterns.name: Puffed-up significance (regression to the mean)
patterns.definition: A modest subject is inflated into a 'pivotal moment' or 'enduring legacy' while the concrete detail that would justify the claim disappears; the subject becomes 'simultaneously less specific and more exaggerated'.
cues: pivotal moment in the evolution of

examples.before: a pivotal moment in the evolution of regional statistics
highlights the enduring legacy of the community's resistance and the transformative power of unity

patterns.notes: 'The most quietly damning tell.' Wikipedia's image: the model 'shouting louder and louder that a portrait shows a uniquely important person, while the portrait itself is fading from a sharp photograph into a blurry, generic sketch'. Academic variant: 'Overgeneralized abstracts that over-emphasize significance without naming specific findings'.

patterns.name: Promotional register for non-promotional subjects
patterns.definition: Travel-brochure or marketing adjectives applied to subjects that are not being sold: heritage, communities, landscapes, legacies.

examples.before: Rich cultural heritage
breathtaking landscapes
enduring legacy
vibrant community
endless possibilities

patterns.notes: Fred Rohrer's Blog. 30-second check: 'Promotional adjectives applied to non-promotional subjects (vibrant community, rich tapestry)'. Journalism variant: product round-ups with 'durable construction', 'excellent value', 'users rave'.

patterns.name: False concession / both-sides hedge
patterns.definition: A symmetrical 'critics say X, supporters say Y, the truth lies in between' move that performs nuance while asserting nothing.
cues: The truth, as is often the case, lies somewhere in between

examples.before: While critics argue X, supporters maintain Y. The truth, as is often the case, lies somewhere in between.

patterns.notes: Ted Chiang, 'ChatGPT Is a Blurry JPEG of the Web': fluency creates 'the illusion that ChatGPT understands the material' while producing 'an approximation' in grammatical form.

patterns.name: Aphoristic closure (pseudo-profound kicker)
patterns.definition: A paragraph or piece ends on a tweetable, pull-quote-shaped sentence that has the shape of wisdom without its friction; a closer that 'sounds like an ending more than it is one'.

examples.before: Because in the end, the real question isn't what AI can do — it's what we will do with it.

patterns.notes: Often built on a negated contrast. In the prize-poem analysis: 'aphorisms that scanned as tweetable', 'optimized for resonance', and 'a closer that sounds like an ending more than it is one'.

patterns.name: Strategic vagueness / abstraction drift
patterns.definition: Well-formed sentences that carry no concrete insight, framing or momentum: generic nouns, hypothetical examples, no one with a last name or regional accent; poems pivot to 'the soul', 'the silence', 'the weight of what remains' instead of a physical image.
patterns.notes: Vauhini Vara: LLM voice is 'polite, predictable, inoffensive, upbeat'; sh-reya.com: 'sounds nice but says very little… no concrete insight, no framing, no momentum'. Claude's poem verdict: 'abstractions that refused to stay concrete'. Counter-move: the Specificity Rewrite.

patterns.name: Sycophancy
patterns.definition: Flattery of the reader or their question before answering; residue of RLHF over-agreeableness.
cues: You're absolutely right to push back on this

examples.before: What a thoughtful question!
You're absolutely right to push back on this
That's a brilliant observation.

patterns.notes: OpenAI conceded in April 2025 that GPT-4o was 'overly flattering or agreeable — often described as sycophantic' and rolled back the update; 'even in retreat, residue remains'. 30-second check: 'Sycophantic opener (Great question! What a thoughtful observation!)'.

patterns.name: False profundity / universal-generic statements
patterns.definition: Low-perplexity truisms stated as insight — claims true of everyone and therefore of no one.
cues: At the end of the day, we are all human.
At the end of the day

examples.before: Everyone has moments of doubt.
Change is the only constant.
At the end of the day, we are all human.

patterns.notes: Chosen 'because they have the lowest cross-entropy loss — they are the safest tokens'.

patterns.name: Flatness of affect (no register shift)
patterns.definition: One tone held for the whole piece; no mood drift from analytical to angry to tender; 'the cadence never varies'.
patterns.notes: Charlie Guo, Artificial Ignorance. Claude specifically 'tends to hold voice more consistently across long documents', which paradoxically makes long-form fiction harder to detect at paragraph level. Fiction cousins: POV lock, pacing flatness.

patterns.name: The missing concrete particular ('collapse of context' / 'no grain')
patterns.definition: Absence of any proper noun, brand name, specific date, month, place, dialect or idiosyncratic detail; the text could be about anywhere and anyone.

examples.before: No Tuesday. No laundromat. No grandmother with a specific brand of mentholated cough drop.

patterns.notes: Laura Preston (n+1) 'collapse of context': the impulse 'to write a speech on the noble savage because noble savage is something you've heard before'. Poetry name: 'No grain: no proper nouns, no specific months, no brand names, no dialect, no idiosyncratic rhythm'. 30-second check: 'Absence of any proper noun, brand name, specific date, or idiosyncratic detail'. Coda: 'be specific, be strange, be where you actually are'.

patterns.name: Tonal sprinkle (cheap warmth at open and close)
patterns.definition: Chatbot ornaments that flank otherwise efficient prose: an eager opener and a helpful closer.
cues: Let me know if you'd like me to go deeper!

examples.before: Hope this helps!
Let me know if you'd like me to go deeper!
Let's dive in, shall we?

patterns.notes: Gmelius: in LLM-assisted emails 'these ornaments colonize the open and close'.

patterns.name: The em dash (additive distribution)
patterns.definition: Em dashes used to attach qualifying or explanatory segments — additive clauses that read like breath cycles — rather than for a sharp parenthetical aside or a dramatic interruption. The diagnostic is the distribution and density, not the presence.
patterns.notes: Model data: ChatGPT, Copilot, Deepseek heavy; Claude used two in Bailey's six-model test (and places them mid-sentence rather than at clause ends); Gemini and Meta.ai none; OpenAI tried to suppress em dashes in GPT-5.1; Reddit tech-subreddit usage roughly tripled 2023–2024. Dissent: Brian Phillips (The Ringer) calls em-dash shaming 'dumb' — 'the most human punctuation mark there is'. 30-second check: 'Em-dashes used additively (attaching qualifiers) rather than disruptively'. Email variant: colons/semicolons replaced by commas or em dashes.

patterns.name: Oxford commas, zero contractions, near-perfect grammar
patterns.definition: Machine cleanliness: consistent serial commas, no contractions, no informality, no odd fragment.
patterns.notes: 'Humans usually slip a dash of informality or the odd fragment' (AI for Lifelong Learners). Register-dependent: formal academic prose legitimately has all three.

patterns.name: Curly quotes and apostrophes in straight-quote contexts
patterns.definition: Typographic (smart) quotes and apostrophes appearing where the surrounding medium uses straight ones — Reddit, code, plain email.
patterns.notes: Models trained on published books render typographical apostrophes by default. Only a tell where the surrounding context is straight-quoted.

patterns.name: Unicode flair in the wrong places
patterns.definition: Bold rendered as Unicode math-bold characters instead of markdown, rightward arrows in non-technical prose, and bullets rendered as the Unicode bullet character.
patterns.notes: Wikipedia's cleanup project flags these as strong tells.

patterns.name: Nested lists for non-list ideas
patterns.definition: Bulleted, especially nested, lists imposed on ideas that are connected or need context and would read better as a paragraph.
patterns.notes: Shreya Shankar: 'LLMs often overuse bullet points, especially nested ones. Lists help when items are parallel and independent, but when ideas are connected or need context, a paragraph is usually better.' Gemini shows 'stronger preference for lists and headings'. 30-second check: 'A bold-stemmed nested bullet list where paragraph prose would do'.

patterns.name: Bold-stemmed bullets with reworded elaboration
patterns.definition: Each bullet opens with a boldfaced stem (label) followed by a sentence that restates the stem in more words.
patterns.notes: Source: 'Bolded bullet stems followed by reworded elaborations'. ChatGPT fingerprint: 'Aggressive use of boldface for list stems'.

patterns.name: Unnecessary H2/H3 headings in short pieces
patterns.definition: Section headings inserted into pieces too short to need navigation.
patterns.notes: Part of the 'bullet-point and heading fetish'; Gemini 'stronger preference for lists and headings'.

patterns.name: Emojis in section headings or as list bullets
patterns.definition: Emoji used as heading decorations or bullet markers.
patterns.notes: 'Residue from RLHF training on marketing blogs.'

patterns.name: Title Case Headings In Surprising Places
patterns.definition: Every word of a heading capitalised where the surrounding house style, medium or language uses sentence case.
patterns.notes: Source gives only the label. In Dutch, German and most non-English languages title case does not exist, so it is a stronger tell there (translationese).

patterns.name: Unrequested rhyme (poetry)
patterns.definition: Rhyme appears in a poem even when no prompt asked for it.
patterns.notes: Walsh, arxiv 2410.15299: 5,700 ChatGPT poems vs 3,700 Poetry Foundation / Academy of American Poets poems; GPT poetry 'much more constrained and uniform than human poetry'.

patterns.name: Quatrain default (poetry)
patterns.definition: Four-line stanzas dominate across forms regardless of what the form wants.
patterns.notes: Walsh, arxiv 2410.15299.

patterns.name: Iambic meter default (poetry)
patterns.definition: Iambic meter used as the default even when unrequested.
patterns.notes: Walsh, arxiv 2410.15299.

patterns.name: First-person plural perspective (poetry)
patterns.definition: Over-representation of 'we / us / our' relative to human-authored poems — a 'curiously dominant' collective voice.
patterns.notes: Walsh finding. Exercise: count first-person-plural pronouns in five ChatGPT poems vs five Poetry Magazine poems.

patterns.name: Poetry signature vocabulary
patterns.definition: A small lexicon that GPT poetry returns to compulsively.
patterns.notes: Walsh, arxiv 2410.15299.

patterns.name: Aphorism density (every line a pull-quote)
patterns.definition: Each line or sentence wants to be extractable as an epigram; no connective tissue between them, only stacked aphorisms.
patterns.notes: Collected by Aranya at Poetly. Also the diagnosis of the prize poem: 'aphorisms that scanned as tweetable'. Poetry-level cousin of aphoristic closure.

patterns.name: Negate-and-redefine at the line level (poetry)
patterns.definition: The negated contrast as a line pair: deny the literal thing, assert the metaphorical one.
cues: Not an ending / but a beginning
I am not water, / I am the thirst.

examples.before: Not an ending / but a beginning
I am not water, / I am the thirst.

patterns.notes: Poetry variant of the negated contrast.

patterns.name: Mood-word accumulation (Instagram-poetry register)
patterns.definition: Emotive abstract-fragile words piled up in place of image.
patterns.notes: 'The training corpus of Instagram poetry and the Poetry Foundation's most-shared pages collapsed into a single register.'

patterns.name: Superficial fidelity to form
patterns.definition: The line count of a form is honoured but its internal rule is not: a 14-line 'sonnet', a 19-line 'villanelle', a 39-line 'sestina' without the sestina's word-end pattern holding.
patterns.notes: 'Formal gestures without formal follow-through' (Walsh).

patterns.name: The uncanny lyric 'I' without a body
patterns.definition: First-person utterance unattached to a situation, a history, a place — an 'I' that is nowhere.
patterns.notes: Poetry tell collected at Poetly.

patterns.name: Dialogue flattening
patterns.definition: All characters sound alike: no distinct idiolect, verbal tics, dialect or pattern of evasion.
patterns.notes: Clarkesworld / Neil Clarke diagnostics.

patterns.name: Parenthetical stage-direction tics
patterns.definition: Dialogue tagged with a bracketed emotion before the line, script-style.

examples.before: Bob: (defensive) Why should I? / Tony: (frustrated) Look…

patterns.notes: Especially GPT-3.5 (David J. Germain, Medium).

patterns.name: 'As-you-know-Bob' exposition
patterns.definition: Mysteries resolved through explanatory speech rather than action; characters tell each other what they both already know.
patterns.notes: Matches the MFA-reader finding 'too much exposition' (Dhillon et al., arxiv 2510.13939).

patterns.name: POV lock
patterns.definition: The narrative 'picks a lane and stays in it with unnatural consistency' — no drift between free indirect style, interior monologue and exterior scene.
patterns.notes: Charlie Guo.

patterns.name: Pacing flatness
patterns.definition: Scenes unfold at a constant rate: no elision, no selective summary, no acceleration.

patterns.name: Mood-saturated weather and rooms (pathetic fallacy)
patterns.definition: Setting details exist only to mirror a character's emotion.

examples.before: The rain pattered softly against the window, mirroring her unspoken grief.

patterns.name: Resolution bias
patterns.definition: Endings tie up; the model does not trust the reader with ambiguity unless explicitly told to.

patterns.name: Mixed or subtly off metaphors
patterns.definition: Metaphors in the right ballpark with the wrong physics: images that do not survive being pictured.

examples.before: The algorithm whispered through the circuits, a river of logic that bloomed in the garden of her mind.

patterns.notes: 30-second check: 'A mixed or slightly-off metaphor in the right ballpark'. Alibaba's literary AI column notes AI editors flag human metaphors as 'confusing' because they resist categorical mapping. MFA-reader study lists 'mixed metaphors' among detection cues.

patterns.name: Clichés, purple prose, lack of subtext
patterns.definition: Stock phrasing and over-ornamented description with nothing beneath the surface — no layers, no subtext.
patterns.notes: Dhillon et al. (arxiv 2510.13939): expert MFA readers detect AI through 'clichés, purple prose, too much exposition, lack of subtext, mixed metaphors' — 'AI-ness in the style'; with fine-tuning these tells can be suppressed and detection accuracy drops. Clarke: 'no subtext or layers'.

patterns.name: Sudden-polish jump (style drift from baseline)
patterns.definition: Diction and syntax leap above the writer's demonstrated baseline in one piece.
patterns.notes: Requires a prior corpus. Author-comparison baselines are 'the most powerful forensic method for suspected individual authors'; the same signal is 'cyborg writing' when Grammarly/autocorrect/LLM polish is stacked. Caution: Waltzer et al. found teachers often flagged better-written essays as AI.

patterns.name: Absence of personal reflection where invited
patterns.definition: Generic claims where the prompt or rubric asked for specifics or first-hand reflection.

patterns.name: Vocabulary/level mismatch
patterns.definition: Register-elevated words out of proportion to the surrounding writing or the writer's history.
patterns.notes: Only a tell relative to a baseline.

patterns.name: Missing or hallucinated citations
patterns.definition: References to pages that do not exist, DOIs that lead nowhere, real journals with wrong volumes/pages, shuffled author lists.
patterns.notes: Student-writing source: Hastewire. Academic source: 'Reference-list oddities: hallucinated citations; real journals with wrong volumes/pages; authors shuffled'. Verify every citation resolves.

patterns.name: Rubric-language echoing
patterns.definition: The text names the assignment rubric's own criteria with suspicious fluency.

patterns.name: One-paste version history
patterns.definition: The entire document arrives in a single paste event in the editor's version history.
patterns.notes: Out-of-text process evidence, not a prose pattern; the source ranks process evidence (version history, oral discussion, drafts) as more defensible than detector scores.

patterns.name: Overgeneralized abstract (significance without findings)
patterns.definition: An abstract that stresses importance and implications but never names a specific result, number or method.
patterns.notes: Domain instance of puffed-up significance.

patterns.name: Fewer engagement markers
patterns.definition: Reduced questions, asides and direct reader address; a less 'interactional' argumentative voice.
patterns.notes: Jiang & Hyland (2025, SAGE): ChatGPT argumentative essays contained significantly fewer engagement markers than human student essays.

patterns.name: Product round-up generic praise
patterns.definition: Round-up articles built from generic adjectival praise with no test, measurement or named user.
patterns.notes: CNET (77 AI articles, corrections on more than half), Sports Illustrated/AdVon, Gannett, G/O Media, BuzzFeed scandals.

patterns.name: Identical paragraph structures across unrelated articles
patterns.definition: The same paragraph template (length, order of moves, closing sentence) repeated across pieces on unrelated subjects.

patterns.name: Missing primary sourcing (unnamed experts)
patterns.definition: Quotes attributed to unidentified 'experts' without names, institutions or contact.

patterns.name: Boilerplate bios of fictional reporters
patterns.definition: Author bylines and biographies for people who do not exist (headshots from AI-portrait marketplaces).
patterns.notes: Sports Illustrated / AdVon Commerce case (Futurism).

patterns.name: Datelines mismatched with events
patterns.definition: Date or place lines that contradict the events described.

patterns.name: Formulaic email opening
patterns.definition: A stock opener that acknowledges nothing specific about the recipient or thread.
cues: I hope this email finds you well

examples.before: I hope this email finds you well

patterns.notes: Gmelius catalog of 'AI-isms'.

patterns.name: Unedited placeholders
patterns.definition: Template variables or bracketed placeholders left in the sent text.

examples.before: Hi {client_name},

patterns.name: Uniform paragraph length (three-sentence, 30–50-word paragraphs)
patterns.definition: Every paragraph is the same size: three sentences, 30–50 words.
patterns.notes: Gmelius. Paragraph-level counterpart of low burstiness.

patterns.name: Absence of colons and semicolons
patterns.definition: Colons and semicolons never appear; their work is done by commas or em dashes.
patterns.notes: Gmelius.

patterns.name: Collaborative closer
patterns.definition: A helpful sign-off offering more assistance, regardless of who wrote to whom.
cues: Please let me know if there's anything else I can help with!

examples.before: Please let me know if there's anything else I can help with!

patterns.notes: Gmelius: appears 'regardless of who sent the email to whom'.

patterns.name: Loss of prior-thread context
patterns.definition: The reply does not actually remember or answer what the earlier message asked.
patterns.notes: Gmelius.

patterns.name: 'Certainly!' / 'Absolutely!' openers
patterns.definition: An enthusiastic one-word acknowledgement opening the response.
patterns.notes: ChatGPT fingerprint; 'aggressively trained down in GPT-5'.

patterns.name: Markdown leaking when not requested
patterns.definition: Headings, bullets, bold and code fences appearing in a plain-text surface (email, comment, chat) that did not ask for markdown.
patterns.notes: ChatGPT fingerprint: 'Tendency to break into markdown when you didn't ask for it'.

patterns.name: First-person assistant self-reference
patterns.definition: The text speaks as a helper about its own helping.
patterns.notes: Claude fingerprint (Context-link.ai; Kenny Kane).

patterns.name: Long multi-clause sentences (Claude) / verbose bulkiness (Gemini)
patterns.definition: Sentences carrying several subordinate clauses with dashes mid-sentence, or verbose, flat rhythms with 'less rhetorical punch' whose errors 'cluster around phrasing bulkiness'.
patterns.notes: Claude: 'Longer sentences with multiple clauses; em-dashes used mid-sentence rather than at clause-ends'. Gemini: 'Verbose, flatter sentence rhythms'.

patterns.name: Redundancy, repetition, lack of coherence
patterns.definition: The same claim restated in different words across paragraphs; connections between paragraphs asserted rather than made.
patterns.notes: 2025 German-medical-essay study: expert detection (70%) was driven by 'redundancy, repetition, and lack of coherence' rather than content familiarity (PMC).

patterns.name: N-gram uniformity / low type-token ratio
patterns.definition: Less diversity in phrase construction: word-triplet transitions are more uniform than Zipf's law predicts, and the ratio of distinct to total n-grams is lower.
patterns.notes: Frohrer blog; computational signal, measurable rather than readable.

methodology.rule: Treat the catalog as a diagnostic field guide, not a tribunal: no single signal is proof of LLM authorship. Human writers use em dashes, say 'delve', build tricolons and close with aphorisms.
The signal lies in clustering, density and texture: judge the co-occurrence of tells and the rate at which they arrive, not any one hit.

30-second field check: treat prose as probabilistically LLM-assisted if three or more of these twelve arrive within a few hundred words — (1) a Kobak focal word (delve, intricate, pivotal, realm, meticulously, navigate, tapestry) in a non-academic context; (2) a 'not X, but Y' construction; (3) a tricolon of parallel short phrases; (4) em dashes used additively rather than disruptively; (5) a closing 'In summary / In conclusion / Ultimately' wrap; (6) uniform sentence length across a paragraph (burstiness < ~0.5); (7) promotional adjectives on non-promotional subjects; (8) a sycophantic opener; (9) orphaned demonstratives; (10) a bold-stemmed nested bullet list where paragraph prose would do; (11) absence of any proper noun, brand name, specific date or idiosyncratic detail; (12) a mixed or slightly-off metaphor.

Delve Audit: over a 500-word sample count every occurrence of the focal list (delve, intricate, meticulously, realm, pivotal, navigate, landscape, tapestry, resonate, testament, underscore, showcasing, compelling, paramount, crucial, foster, elevate, surpass), plot the density, and judge whether the piece sits inside the 'excess band'.
Count signposting filler phrases per 500 words; the higher the count, the darker the probability.
Burstiness contrast: chart sentence length sentence by sentence and compare the curve against a human passage (Dillard, Baldwin, Ruefle); flat curves are the tell, spiky ones are human.

Computational signals in order of rigor: corpus-level excess vocabulary (Kobak; quantifies population penetration but cannot identify individual documents), perplexity + burstiness (GPTZero and most commercial detectors), n-gram uniformity, type-token ratio, stylometric fingerprinting of specific models, and author-comparison against a known prior corpus (the most powerful method for an individual author; style drift is diagnostic).
First-person plural check (poetry): count we/us/our and compare against published human poems.

Do not flag em dashes on presence; flag only the additive distribution (qualifiers attached like breath cycles). Human writers use them for sharp asides and dramatic interruptions, and Brian Phillips calls the em dash 'the most human punctuation mark there is'.

Non-native English writers naturally produce lower-perplexity text: seven detectors misclassified 61.3% of TOEFL essays as AI (19.8% unanimously) against near-perfect accuracy on US eighth-grade essays. Never treat low perplexity or uniform rhythm as decisive for ESL writers.

Neurodivergent writers (autism, ADHD, dyslexia) often write in repetitive or highly structured patterns, and heavy Grammarly users get their text 'normalized'; both trip detectors ('cyborg writing'). 15 of 17 flagged students in one UC Davis class were false positives; a deaf, precise writer was accused of being a chatbot about a dozen times in five months.
Well-written text is not evidence of AI: teachers 'often flagged better-written essays as AI', and rater confidence was uncorrelated with accuracy (Waltzer et al. 2023: teachers 70%, students 62%).
Inline citations are a potential non-tell (Perplexity adds them by default); their presence should not count for or against.

Model fingerprints drift continuously: patterns found in earlier ChatGPT versions had shrunk or disappeared in newer models (Reinhart); sycophantic openers, 'Certainly!' and em dashes have all been actively suppressed. Re-weight model-specific tells by date.

Detectors are unreliable in absolute terms: OpenAI retired its classifier at 26% accuracy on AI text and 9% false positives on human text; Turnitin's claimed sub-1% false-positive rate was contradicted by a 50% false-positive sample; humans detect at 53–70%, heavy daily LLM users at ~90%.

Distinguish generated from assisted: brainstormed, outlined, rephrased, copyedited or translated text may be 80% human and 20% machine or the reverse, and no current method separates 'generated' from 'polished', 'restructured' or 'translated with assistance' (detectors collapsed across five grades of AI involvement).

Never use a detector score as evidence in a high-stakes context (grades, hiring, accusations); prefer writing-process evidence — version history, oral discussion of the piece, drafts. A flag cannot be disproved and the social cost of a false accusation is not abstract.

This guide is descriptive, not an evasion manual: the cat-and-mouse tricks it reports (prompting for varied sentence length, inserting anecdotes, 'in the style of' a named human, humanizer tools such as GPTinf/NetusAI/Walter Writes, adding 'cheeky' to a prompt) are listed as the reason detection fails, not as a method to apply.

Do not fake humanity by inserting deliberate typos, fragments or infelicities; the source calls this the 'paranoia spiral' — 'signal-jamming of human writing itself'. The counter-move is specificity, not performed sloppiness.
Negation Hunt (rewrite mode): for every 'not X, but Y' construction, rewrite it as a direct affirmative, then check what was lost and what was gained.

Specificity Rewrite: replace every general noun ('people', 'community', 'technology', 'change') with a specific one ('my grandmother', 'the Christiansburg Kroger', 'the 2017 iPhone X', 'the layoffs of March 2020'). 'This is the pedagogical counter-move.'

Be specific, be strange, be where you actually are: human badness is particular to one person, LLM badness is generic, so the defence against AI prose is grain — a Tuesday, a laundromat, a brand of cough drop, a last name, a regional accent.

Let the register move: a human writer drifts mid-piece from analytical to angry to tender, bursts short sentences against long ones, and lets the odd fragment or comma splice stand. Hold no single temperature.
Match the author's demonstrated baseline; a sudden polish jump in diction or syntax above prior work is the drift signal, and the same comparison is what holds up in an integrity hearing.

Weigh focal words and 'In conclusion' wraps by context: the 30-second check counts a Kobak word only 'in a non-academic context', and Oxford commas, zero contractions and perfect grammar are native to formal academic prose.
Use a list only when items are parallel and independent; when ideas are connected or need context, write a paragraph (Shankar).

Verify every citation resolves: page exists, DOI leads somewhere, journal volume and pages match, author order is right. Hallucinated and shuffled references are a hard tell in student and academic writing.
Check sourcing and datelines in journalism: named experts with institutions, real bylines, dates that match the events described.

Domain-specific tolerance: poetry tells (unrequested rhyme, quatrains, iambic default, we/us/our, heart/embrace/echo/whisper, sonnet/villanelle/sestina line counts without the form's internal rule) and fiction tells (dialogue flattening, stage-direction tags, as-you-know-Bob exposition, POV lock, pacing flatness, mood-saturated weather, resolution bias, off metaphors) only apply inside those genres.

Model-specific fingerprints (aidiolects): ChatGPT — heaviest em dashes, intro + triplet + recap, 'Certainly!/Absolutely!', bold list stems, negated contrast, unrequested markdown. Claude — long multi-clause sentences, mid-sentence em dashes, hedging register, first-person self-reference, cautious about factuality, less tricolon, consistent voice. Gemini — verbose flat rhythm, fewer em dashes, more lists and headings, bulky phrasing. Copilot/Deepseek ChatGPT-adjacent; Perplexity adds inline citations.
Report a diagnosis as probabilistic and descriptive, listing the co-occurring tells and their density, never as a verdict ('not a gotcha but a descriptive one').

Critical vocabulary the source establishes: 'AI slop' (surface polish with nothing underneath), 'AI-ese' (overly formal helpful tone, perfectly structured sentences, peculiar vocabulary), 'aidiolect' (model-specific dialect), 'delve-speak', 'cyborg writing' (mixed tool-use text), 'lossy compression' (Chiang), 'regression to the mean' (Wikipedia's term for puffing-up), 'collapse of context' (Preston), 'simulator/simulacra' (Janus, Denicola).

Extracted 83 patterns and 32 methodology rules. Kobak excess words and the 21 focal words are kept as two lists because they come from two papers and differ; the 18-word Delve-Audit subset and the 7-word field-check subset are recorded in notes. 'Bullet-point and heading fetish' was split into nested lists, bold-stemmed bullets and unnecessary headings because a rewriter acts on them separately; likewise the bad-subject problem and orphaned demonstratives. Poetry 'no grain' and 'abstraction drift' were folded into the prose patterns 'missing concrete particular' and 'strategic vagueness' with their cues, since the source names the same mechanism in two domains; student and academic hallucinated citations were folded into one pattern; ChatGPT's 'intro + triplet + closing recap' is recorded on the five-paragraph-shape pattern; 'paragraph tricolons' on the tricolon; email 'commas or em dashes replacing colons' on both the em-dash and the absence-of-colons patterns. Left out as not extractable into a rewriting skill: the biographical and reception material in section X (Chiang, Vara, Preston, Hsu, Sloan, Clarke, Trott bios; magazine submission policies; the Diagram chapbook controversy; Wikipedia's G15 criterion), the detection-scandal narratives in VI.E beyond the tells they yield, the 'détournement' suggestion that tells can be creative material, and the reader comment. 'Inability to discuss one's own essay aloud' and 'one-paste version history' are process evidence, not prose; the first is in the gates rule, the second kept as an artifacts pattern with a note. Curly apostrophes in the source's phrases were normalized to straight in cues so a regex author can use them; the curly-quote pattern keeps the typographic characters. Nothing in the source resisted classification, but the forensic signals of section VIII (perplexity, burstiness, n-gram uniformity, type-token ratio, stylometry, author baselines) sit between pattern and scoring, so they appear as both a scoring rule and, where they describe a readable property of the text, a pattern.
